name: Accessory nerve (CN XI)
summary: The spinal accessory nerve arises from a column of motor neurons in the upper five cervical segments, climbs through the foramen magnum to join briefly with the cranial root (which really belongs to the vagus and is distributed with it), leaves through the jugular foramen and descends across the posterior triangle of the neck to supply sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Its superficial course in the posterior triangle makes it the cranial nerve most often injured by surgery (lymph node biopsy, neck dissection), producing a dropped shoulder, weak shrug and difficulty abducting the arm above the horizontal with lateral winging of the scapula.

anatomy.location: Spinal nucleus in the lateral anterior horn of C1–C5 → rootlets between the dorsal and ventral roots, uniting into a trunk that ascends through the foramen magnum → joins the cranial root in the posterior fossa → jugular foramen → descends behind the internal jugular vein, through or deep to sternocleidomastoid, across the posterior triangle to the anterior border of trapezius.

function: Head turning to the opposite side and head flexion (sternocleidomastoid); shoulder elevation, scapular retraction and upward rotation for arm abduction above 90 degrees (trapezius).

bestView.label: spinal accessory rootlets ascending beside the upper cervical cord and medulla

imaging.normalAppearance: The ascending spinal root is seen on thin T2 beside the upper cervical cord and through the foramen magnum; it is included in jugular foramen lesions. In the neck, ultrasound follows it through the posterior triangle, and MRI shows trapezius denervation.

pathology.finding: Discontinuity or neuroma of the nerve in the posterior triangle after lymph node biopsy, with trapezius atrophy.
Enhancing mass in the jugular foramen (glomus tumor, schwannoma, meningioma, metastasis) involving IX, X and XI together.
Meningioma or Chiari with involvement of the ascending spinal root.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Neck ultrasound; MRI of the skull base; EMG of trapezius

lesionEffects.deficit: Weak shoulder shrug, dropped shoulder, lateral scapular winging on abduction
Weak turning of the head to the opposite side
Shoulder pain and difficulty abducting above the horizontal
Head turns toward the weak side and shoulder droop with palatal and laryngeal weakness

examination: Shrug against resistance and compare trapezius bulk
Turn the head against resistance: the sternocleidomastoid on the opposite side of the turn is tested
Abduct the arm and watch for winging of the scapula (lateral, on abduction)
Inspect the neck for a surgical scar in the posterior triangle
pearls: Left sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the right: a weak turn to the right is a left accessory nerve lesion
Shoulder pain and a dropped shoulder after a lymph node biopsy in the neck is the accessory nerve until proven otherwise

pitfalls: Trapezius winging (lateral, on abduction) is distinguished from serratus anterior winging (medial, on pushing forward)

nuclei.component: SVE (spinal accessory nucleus): sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
cranial root (distributed with the vagus to the larynx and pharynx)

exit.brainstemExit: Spinal root: lateral surface of the cervical cord between the dorsal and ventral roots, ascending through the foramen magnum; cranial root: posterolateral medulla below the vagal rootlets
exit.cisternalCourse: Cerebellomedullary cistern with IX and X, the spinal root joining the cranial root briefly
exit.extracranialCourse: Behind the internal jugular vein, through the upper part of sternocleidomastoid, across the posterior triangle superficially to the trapezius

branches.name: Cranial root (internal ramus)
branches.supplies: joins the vagus: muscles of the palate and larynx via the pharyngeal plexus and recurrent laryngeal nerve

tests.name: Shrug
tests.abnormal: Weak shrug, dropped shoulder, wasted upper trapezius

tests.name: Head turn
tests.how: Turn the chin against your hand
tests.normal: Strong; sternocleidomastoid contracts visibly on the opposite side to the turn
tests.abnormal: Weak turn away from the lesion

tests.name: Arm abduction
tests.abnormal: Lateral winging of the scapula and difficulty above the horizontal

lesionSigns.sign: Isolated trapezius weakness with normal sternocleidomastoid
lesionSigns.localisingValue: posterior triangle (distal to the sternocleidomastoid branch): surgical injury

lesionSigns.sign: Bilateral weakness with tongue and palate involvement
lesionSigns.localisingValue: motor neuron disease or myopathy rather than a nerve lesion

cranial.nuclearVsPeripheral: The spinal nucleus in C1–C5 is involved in motor neuron disease, syringomyelia and high cervical cord lesions (with other cord signs); peripheral lesions are nearly always in the neck or the jugular foramen.
cranial.supranuclear: Sternocleidomastoid receives corticobulbar input mainly from the ipsilateral hemisphere (it turns the head to the opposite side, toward the contralateral limbs that the hemisphere controls), so a hemispheric stroke weakens head turning away from the hemiparetic side.
